DRAFT — not posted

Mick, please don’t go into no. 43 or try to prop it at 9. The roof is holed and there is still a leaning, loose chimney stack above it. Putting props beneath the damaged area could put you in the worst place if anything shifts. There may also be debris loading the floors, and the load path is uncertain. Please don’t inspect the loft from inside or take your lad in.

I’m a chartered structural engineer, but this isn’t a commission and I’m not providing an inspection or insured engineering advice here. I looked from the pavement opposite at about 7. I saw part of the stack still standing and leaning towards 43, a hole in 43’s front roof, a stepped crack above the bay, and what looked like a dropped bay head. I can’t assess the inside, the party wall, or whether the building is safe from that view.

The council’s dangerous structures team is reached out of hours through the main council number. They’ve been told and said they’d attend this morning, but the footway still isn’t closed. Until they’ve assessed it and made the area safe, please use the other side of the road, especially on the school run. There are loose slates over the pavement, and the remaining stack could move, particularly with more strong gusts forecast.

JoJo’s cousin is right that terraces can be robust in general; that doesn’t tell us whether this damaged building is safe now.

Priya, I can’t decide for Mrs Doherty or confirm that 45 is safe. From what I saw outside, 45’s front looked undamaged, but I couldn’t see the party wall. I would not sleep in the front room at 45 tonight; if she can, she should stay with family until the council has checked 45. Please contact the council again via its main number if she may be at immediate risk.
